Transient Learning Dynamics Drive Escape from Sharp Valleys in Stochastic Gradient Descent

Ning Yang Thanks: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Peking University Chengdu Academy for Advanced Interdisciplinary Biotechnologies, Chengdu 610213, China    Yikuan Zhang Thanks: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: School of Physics, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China    Qi Ouyang Affiliation: Institute for Advanced Study in Physics, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310058, China    Chao Tang Affiliation: Peking University Chengdu Academy for Advanced Interdisciplinary Biotechnologies, Chengdu 610213, China Affiliation: Center for Quantitative Biology, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China    Yuhai Tu Email: ytu@flatironinstitute.org Affiliation: Center for Computational Biology & Center for Computational Neuroscience, Flatiron Institute, New York, NY 10010, USA
Abstract

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is central to deep learning, yet the dynamical origin of its preference for flatter, more generalizable solutions remains unclear. Here, by analyzing SGD learning dynamics, we identify a nonequilibrium mechanism governing solution selection. Numerical experiments reveal a transient exploratory phase in which SGD trajectories repeatedly escape sharp valleys and transition toward flatter regions of the loss landscape. By using a tractable physical model, we show that the SGD noise reshapes the landscape into an effective potential that favors flat solutions. Crucially, we uncover a transient freezing mechanism: as training proceeds, growing energy barriers suppress inter-valley transitions and ultimately trap the dynamics within a single basin. Increasing the SGD noise strength delays this freezing, which enhances convergence to flatter minima. Together, these results provide a unified physical framework linking learning dynamics, loss-landscape geometry, and generalization, and suggest principles for the design of more effective optimization algorithms.

I Introduction

Despite its substantial empirical success across numerous fields, the underlying mechanisms of deep learning remain poorly understood [1, 2]. The training of a deep neural network can be viewed as the optimization of a high-dimensional loss landscape in parameter space [3, 4, 5], formally expressed as

ℒ⁡(𝜽)=1M​∑i=1Ml⁡(𝒔i,𝜽),\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}l(\bm{s}_{i};\bm{\theta}), (1)

where l⁡(𝒔i,𝜽)l(\bm{s}_{i};\bm{\theta}) denotes the loss associated with a single training sample 𝒔i\bm{s}_{i} from a dataset of size MM, and 𝜽\bm{\theta} represents the network’s parameter vector.

A prevailing hypothesis posits that the geometry of this loss landscape is intrinsically linked to the model’s generalization ability [6, 7]. Specifically, solutions residing in “flat” or “wide” minima tend to generalize well to unseen data, whereas those in “sharp” or “narrow” minima are more prone to overfitting [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Recently, the relation between flatness of loss landscape at a solution with its generalization has been shown explicitly via an exact activity-weight duality [14]. This flatness-generalization relation has led to the widespread view that the effectiveness of an optimizer is closely tied to its ability to locate flat minima.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is the core optimizer of modern deep learning [15, 16]; despite its simplicity, it enables neural networks to achieve strong generalization. Unlike full-batch Gradient Descent (GD), which computes gradients over the entire dataset, SGD estimates the gradient using a randomly sampled mini-batch {𝒔μi}i=1B\{\bm{s}_{\mu_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{B}, μi∈{1,⋯,M}{\mu_{i}\in\{1,\cdots,M\}} of size BB. The corresponding mini-batch loss is defined as

ℒμ​(𝜽)=1B​∑i=1Bl⁡(𝒔μi,𝜽),\mathcal{L}^{\mu}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}l(\bm{s}_{\mu_{i}};\bm{\theta}), (2)

and the parameter update at iteration tt follows

𝜽t+1=𝜽t−η​∇𝜽ℒμ​(𝜽t),\bm{\theta}_{t+1}=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\eta\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}^{\mu}\left(\bm{\theta}_{t}\right), (3)

where η\eta denotes the learning rate.

Due to mini-batch sampling, the noise covariance in SGD aligns with the Hessian matrix, making the noise both landscape-dependent and anisotropic [17, 18]. This anisotropic stochasticity is believed to bias optimization trajectories toward flatter regions of the loss landscape [19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. Empirical studies further indicate that increasing the overall noise strength of SGD—by raising the learning rate η\eta or reducing the batch size BB—typically leads to convergence toward flatter minima with improved generalization [12, 24, 10]. In this view, gradient noise acts as an implicit regularizer, enabling the optimizer to escape sharp minima and explore broader regions of parameter space. However, most previous analyses studied this implicit regularization when the loss landscape can be approximated as a degenerate valley with negligible gradients [20, 21, 25, 23]. While this approximation holds in the late stages of training, the transient dynamics by which SGD selects flatter solutions during the early phase remain poorly understood.

Multiple studies have demonstrated the critical importance of the early phase of training, showing that key properties of the final network are established long before convergence [26, 27, 28, 29, 30]. For instance, the “lottery ticket hypothesis” suggests that trainable subnetworks emerge very early in the training process [31]. This raises a crucial question: How does SGD navigate the complex, high-dimensional loss landscape during these formative early stages to set the trajectory toward generalizable solutions? Understanding this “early transient dynamic” is essential for a complete theory of deep learning optimization.

In this paper, we systematically study how stochastic gradient descent (SGD) escapes sharp minima and preferentially converges toward flatter regions during early training when there are significant down-hill gradients. Combining empirical observations with a tractable theoretical model, we characterize the transient dynamics underlying this behavior. We identify a stochastic “valley-jumping” mechanism that enables SGD to explore multiple basins of attraction in the initial phase of optimization.

Our study provides a clear physical picture of transient learning dynamics. Anisotropic noise in SGD reshapes the loss landscape, giving rise to an emergent effective potential that systematically biases the dynamics toward flatter, more generalizable minima. Crucially, this exploratory behavior is intrinsically transient: as training proceeds, the evolving landscape geometry dynamically “freezes” the trajectory into a single valley. Higher noise levels—arising from larger learning rates or smaller batch sizes—prolong this pre-freezing regime, allowing the dynamics more time to follow the effective potential and discover flatter solutions. Taken together, these results offer a unified framework connecting stochasticity, loss landscape geometry, and generalization, and reveal an explicitly transient mechanism by which SGD preferentially selects flat minima.

II Results

II.1 SGD converges to distinct loss valleys separated by barriers

To characterize the loss landscape explored by stochastic gradient descent (SGD), we first examine the endpoints of optimization. Starting from an identical initialization, we performed multiple training runs that differed only in random seed, batch size, and learning rate, using a 1,000-sample subset of the MNIST classification task and a fully connected neural network with two hidden layers (see Sec. I A in Supplemental Material for details).

The resulting training trajectories are shown in Fig. 1A, projected onto the first two principal components of the network parameters. Rather than converging to a single point, the trajectories cluster into several well-separated regions of parameter space, which we identify as distinct valleys of the loss landscape. All trajectories shown have fully converged and achieve 100% training accuracy, indicating that each cluster corresponds to a local minimum separated from others by loss barriers.

Pairwise Jaccard similarity analysis, computed at the fully converged endpoints, further confirmed this clustered structure (Fig. 1B), defined as

SimJ​(𝜽(i),𝜽(j))≡|ℰ⁡(𝜽(i))∩ℰ⁡(𝜽(j))||ℰ⁡(𝜽(i))∪ℰ⁡(𝜽(j))|,\mathrm{Sim}_{J}(\bm{\theta}^{(i)},\bm{\theta}^{(j)})\equiv\frac{\bigl|\mathcal{E}(\bm{\theta}^{(i)})\cap\mathcal{E}(\bm{\theta}^{(j)})\bigr|}{\bigl|\mathcal{E}(\bm{\theta}^{(i)})\cup\mathcal{E}(\bm{\theta}^{(j)})\bigr|}, (4)

where ℰ⁡(𝜽(i))\mathcal{E}(\bm{\theta}^{(i)}) denotes the set of misclassified test samples for solution 𝜽(i)\bm{\theta}^{(i)}. Unlike similarity measures defined directly in weight space, which suffer from permutation symmetry of neurons, this error-based similarity is invariant to such symmetries and thus provides a more faithful measure of solution similarity. Finally, Hessian spectra computed at these endpoints provide additional evidence for the valley structure: a few near-zero eigenvalues correspond to flat directions along the valley floor, while many large eigenvalues indicate steep walls (see Sec. I B in Supplemental Material and Fig. S1), consistent with previous studies [11, 32, 24].

These valleys are not smoothly connected but are separated by substantial loss barriers. Linear interpolation between two final solutions, 𝜽(i)\bm{\theta}^{(i)} and 𝜽(j)\bm{\theta}^{(j)}, demonstrates this separation. To quantify this effect, we define the loss barrier Δ​ℒbarrier\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{barrier}} as

Δ​ℒbarrier​(𝜽(i),𝜽(j))≡maxα∈[0,1]⁡ℒ⁡(α​𝜽(i)+(1−α)​𝜽(j))−ℒ⁡(𝜽(i))+ℒ⁡(𝜽(j))2,\begin{split}\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{barrier}}(\bm{\theta}^{(i)},\bm{\theta}^{(j)})&\equiv\max_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\mathcal{L}\!\left(\alpha\bm{\theta}^{(i)}+(1-\alpha)\bm{\theta}^{(j)}\right)\\[6.0pt] &\quad-\frac{\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}^{(i)})+\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}^{(j)})}{2},\end{split} (5)

where α\alpha is the interpolation coefficient. For highly similar solutions (S​i​mJ=0.95Sim_{J}=0.95), the interpolation path exhibits a negligible barrier (Fig. 1C). In contrast, dissimilar solutions (S​i​mJ=0.625Sim_{J}=0.625) are separated by a pronounced barrier that must be crossed to move from one valley to another (Fig. 1D). Tracking these interpolation paths over training time further shows that such barriers emerge early in the optimization process.

Moreover, this trend is robust: plotting barrier height against solution similarity across many pairs reveals a clear negative correlation, indicating that more dissimilar solutions are separated by higher loss barriers (Fig. 1E; linear fit R2=0.64R^{2}=0.64). Together, these results depict the neural network loss landscape as a complex terrain of multiple valleys, separated by barriers whose heights reflect the functional dissimilarity of the solutions they contain.

II.2 Increased SGD noise promotes convergence to flatter, more generalizable valleys

Stochasticity in SGD arises primarily from mini-batch sampling, with its magnitude controlled by the batch size BB and learning rate η\eta: smaller BB or larger η\eta produce stronger noise [10]. To systematically access its effects, we trained networks over a broad range of (η,B)(\eta,B) combinations, spanning learning rates from η=0.001\eta=0.001 to 0.10.1 and batch sizes from B=10B=10 to 1,0001{,}000, where the latter corresponds to full-batch gradient descent. For each parameter setting, we performed 20 independent training runs starting from identical initial conditions (see Sec. I A in Supplemental Material).

As expected, increased SGD noise led to more diverse final solutions. This diversity is captured quantitatively by the average pairwise Jaccard similarity ⟨S​i​mJ⟩\langle Sim_{J}\rangle between independent realizations for each hyperparameter setting (Fig. 2A). Low-noise settings (large BB, small η\eta) produced solutions that were highly similar, whereas higher noise (smaller BB or larger η\eta) systematically reduced ⟨S​i​mJ⟩\langle Sim_{J}\rangle, indicating broader exploration of the loss landscape. This trend is further visualized in PCA-projected weight space: the training trajectories for a low-noise example (B=50,η=0.01B=50,\eta=0.01, ① in Fig. 2A) cluster tightly (Fig. 2B), whereas the high-noise example (B=50,η=0.05B=50,\eta=0.05, ② in Fig. 2A) spreads over a wider region of PCA space (Fig. 2C), highlighting the role of noise in enabling broader exploration.

Crucially, this exploration is biased toward more generalizable solutions: higher noise systematically yielded solutions with higher maximum test accuracy max⁡(A​c​ctest)\max(Acc_{\mathrm{test}}) (Fig. 2D). These higher-performing solutions also lie in flatter valleys: here, we quantified flatness FF as the inverse geometric mean of the top NN non-degenerate Hessian eigenvalues,

F≡(∏i=1Nλi​(𝐇))−1N,F\equiv\left(\prod_{i=1}^{N}\lambda_{i}(\mathbf{H})\right)^{-\tfrac{1}{N}}, (6)

where we set N=10N=10 for the 10-class MNIST task [33]. Increasing noise consistently steered optimization toward flatter minima (Fig. 2F). Direct comparisons further confirmed that smaller BB yields solutions that are both flatter and more accurate (Fig. 2E&G), reinforcing the well-established link between flatness and generalization [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13].

Overall, these results indicate that SGD noise functions not merely as an implicit regularizer but as an active exploration mechanism: by promoting broader exploration of the parameter space, higher noise systematically guides optimization toward flatter valleys associated with improved generalization.

II.3 Larger SGD noise extends the transient search phase of training

Having established that SGD noise biases optimization toward flatter, more generalizable valleys, we next examine the learning dynamics underlying this effect. Training typically begins with a rapid decrease in the loss, corresponding to a transient search phase during which the optimizer explores multiple regions of the loss landscape. We define the end of this phase as the freezing time, tfreezet_{\mathrm{freeze}}, given by the first iteration at which the training loss drops below a small threshold ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c}:

tfreeze≡min⁡{t∣ℒtrain​(t)<ℒc}.t_{\mathrm{freeze}}\equiv\min\{\,t\mid\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(t)<\mathcal{L}_{c}\,\}. (7)

In our experiments, we set ℒc=0.1\mathcal{L}_{c}=0.1; varying this threshold does not affect the qualitative conclusions (see Sec. I D in Supplemental Material and Fig. S3). Beyond tfreezet_{\mathrm{freeze}}, training accuracy approaches 100%, and the dynamics become confined to the basin of attraction of a single valley (Fig. 3A).

We then investigated how SGD noise influences the duration of this transient exploration phase. While different noise levels (controlled via batch size BB) lead to comparable final training losses, higher noise systematically delays entry into the low-loss regime. In particular, reducing BB increases tfreezet_{\mathrm{freeze}} (Fig. 3B), indicating that optimizers with larger noise spend more time exploring the landscape before settling into a valley. A phase map of the normalized freezing time, η​⟨tfreeze⟩\eta\langle t_{\mathrm{freeze}}\rangle (where η\eta sets the iteration time interval), across a wide hyperparameter range further confirms this trend: the duration of the early transient phase consistently grows with increased SGD noise (Fig. 3C).

Importantly, this extended exploration period is not wasted. It is precisely during this phase that the optimizer discovers flatter regions of the landscape. Tracking the evolution of flatness during training shows a continuous increase (except at the very beginning, where gradients are extremely large) across all noise levels (Fig. 3D). Notably, high-noise trajectories (small BB) not only prolong the exploration period but also leverage it to locate progressively flatter regions, ultimately converging to solutions with substantially greater flatness than their low-noise counterparts.

These results establish a direct link between the duration of the noise-driven transient phase and the geometric quality of the final solution: the longer the optimizer explores before freezing, the flatter the valley it is likely to reach.

II.4 Continuation training experiments reveal valley escapes during early transient phase

To directly visualize how SGD transitions between valleys, we designed a continuation training experiment. A network was first trained using SGD to generate a reference trajectory (Fig. 4A; reference setting B=50B=50, η=0.05\eta=0.05). At selected times tct_{c} along this trajectory, training was branched and resumed using full-batch gradient descent (GD) with the same learning rate. Because GD is deterministic, it rapidly descends into the local valley specified by its initialization, without further stochastic exploration. The final solutions obtained from these continuations therefore identify the valley occupied by the SGD trajectory at time tct_{c} (Fig. 4A; see Sec. I E in Supplemental Material for details). This procedure enables a direct reconstruction of the sequence of valleys explored by SGD during the early stages of training.

The results provide direct evidence for valley jumping during the early stages of training. Continuations from very early times (e.g., tc=20t_{c}=20) converge to solutions characterized by high test loss and low flatness (Fig. 4B, C). As tct_{c} increases, however, the trajectories branched at later times progressively converge to better solutions, landing in valleys with both lower test loss and higher flatness (inset of Fig. 4B, C). This indicates that the SGD trajectory does not remain trapped in its initial basin of attraction, but instead transitions across the landscape to discover flatter and more generalizable regions. The improvement is systematic: the final test loss and flatness of these solutions are strongly correlated (R2=0.76R^{2}=0.76), confirming that the search for flatter valleys is effectively the search for better generalization (Fig. 4D).

We further found that valley jumping occurs almost exclusively before the freezing time tfreezet_{\mathrm{freeze}}. To quantify this effect, we computed the Jaccard similarity S​i​mJSim_{J} between final solutions obtained from different continuation times. Similarities remain low between solutions at early continuation times but increase steadily, approaching 1 as tct_{c} nears tfreezet_{\mathrm{freeze}} (Fig. 4E). This pattern indicates that substantial transitions between distinct valleys occur almost entirely during the transient phase of training. Once this phase is surpassed (tc≥tfreezet_{c}\geq t_{\mathrm{freeze}}, red square region in Fig. 4E), the SGD trajectory stabilizes and remains confined to a single, high-quality valley.

Together, these results from the continuation training experiments indicate that SGD drives valley transitions during the transient phase, guiding the trajectory to escape from sharper minima and progressively converge into flatter, more generalizable ones.

II.5 A minimal two-valley model recapitulates empirical training dynamics

As described above, in real training we empirically observe the following features: (1) the loss landscape splits into multiple solution valleys originating from a common starting point, each characterized by a different degree of flatness; (2) as training proceeds and the loss decreases, the valleys become increasingly flatter, reflecting a systematic growth of flatness; (3) due to stochastic mini-batch sampling, the SGD trajectory may transiently jump from shaper valleys during the early phase of optimization; and (4) increasing the level of SGD noise systematically delays the valley-jumping freezing time, thereby biasing the dynamics toward convergence into the flatter valley. This physical picture is schematically illustrated in Fig. 5A, which bears a strong resemblance to the Waddington epigenetic landscape where cells traverse a bifurcating potential surface to achieve stable developmental fates [34, 35, 36, 37, 38].

To explain these phenomena within a minimal yet analytically tractable framework, we construct a two-dimensional loss landscape ℒ⁡(x,y)\mathcal{L}(x,y) that takes the form of a bifurcating valley (Fig. 5B). Here, the variable yy represents the principal training direction along which the overall loss decreases, whereas xx denotes a symmetry-breaking parameter direction where the valley bifurcation emerges. The loss is defined piecewise as

ℒ⁡(x,y)=ℒ0​(y)+{x​(x−g1​(y))f1​(y),x≥0,x​(x+g2​(y))f2​(y),x<0,\mathcal{L}(x,y)=\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)+\begin{cases}\dfrac{x(x-g_{1}(y))}{f_{1}(y)},&x\geq 0,\\ \dfrac{x(x+g_{2}(y))}{f_{2}(y)},&x<0,\end{cases} (8)

with several components controlling the landscape geometry. The functions g1,2​(y)g_{1,2}(y) set the valley positions:

g1​(y)=2​x1​yy+yb,g2​(y)=2​x2​yy+yb,g_{1}(y)=\frac{2x_{1}y}{y+y_{b}},\qquad g_{2}(y)=\frac{2x_{2}y}{y+y_{b}}, (9)

so that the valley minima x1,2⋆x_{1,2}^{\star} are located at x1⋆=g1​(y)/2x_{1}^{\star}=g_{1}(y)/2 and x2⋆=−g2(y)/2x_{2}^{\star}=-g_{2}(y)/2, asymptotically approaching x1x_{1} and −x2-x_{2} as y→∞y\to\infty. The parameter yby_{b} sets the bifurcation scale, controlling how rapidly the valleys separate. The valley flatness (inverse curvatures) are determined by f1,2​(y)f_{1,2}(y):

f1​(y)=f0​x12x02​(y+yf)2(y+yb)2,f2​(y)=f0​x22x02​(y+yf)2(y+yb)2,f_{1}(y)=f_{0}\frac{x_{1}^{2}}{x_{0}^{2}}\frac{(y+y_{f})^{2}}{(y+y_{b})^{2}},\qquad f_{2}(y)=f_{0}\frac{x_{2}^{2}}{x_{0}^{2}}\frac{(y+y_{f})^{2}}{(y+y_{b})^{2}}, (10)

where f0f_{0} sets the overall flatness scale, x0x_{0} is a normalization constant, and yfy_{f} controls the rate at which both valleys flatten as yy increases. Note that while the absolute flatness evolves, their ratio remains constant. We define this flatness ratio as γ≡f1​(y)/f2​(y)=(x1/x2)2\gamma\equiv f_{1}(y)/f_{2}(y)=(x_{1}/x_{2})^{2}. Since x1>x2x_{1}>x_{2}, we have γ>1\gamma>1, indicating that the valley with x>0x>0 is flatter.

For simplicity, the landscape is constructed to disentangle the geometric effect of flatness from valley depth. The two minima, located at x1⋆​(y)x^{\star}_{1}(y) and x2⋆​(y)x^{\star}_{2}(y), are designed to have equal depths relative to the barrier at x=0x=0. This common depth defines the barrier height Δ​ℒ​(y)\Delta\mathcal{L}(y), which evolves with yy according to

Δ​ℒ​(y)=ℒ⁡(0,y)−ℒ⁡(x1⋆,y)=ℒ⁡(0,y)−ℒ⁡(x2⋆,y)=x02f0​y2(y+yf)2.\begin{split}\Delta\mathcal{L}(y)&=\mathcal{L}(0,y)-\mathcal{L}(x_{1}^{\star},y)=\mathcal{L}(0,y)-\mathcal{L}(x_{2}^{\star},y)\\ &=\frac{x_{0}^{2}}{f_{0}}\frac{y^{2}}{(y+y_{f})^{2}}.\end{split} (11)

The barrier height increases with yy and saturates at x02/f0x_{0}^{2}/f_{0} as y→∞y\to\infty. Furthermore, we introduce a global drift term

ℒ0(y)=ℒde−y/yd+ℒ0⋆,\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)=\mathcal{L}_{d}e^{-y/y_{d}}+\mathcal{L}_{0}^{\star}, (12)

which adds a weak, decaying bias along the yy-direction and captures the overall loss reduction typically induced by the cross-entropy function during training. Here, ℒd\mathcal{L}_{d} controls the initial bias strength and ydy_{d} sets its decay scale along yy. A constant offset ℒ0⋆=x02/f0\mathcal{L}_{0}^{\star}=x_{0}^{2}/f_{0} is included to ensure that ℒ≥0\mathcal{L}\geq 0 across the entire landscape.

The learning dynamics are described by a discrete-time Langevin equation. At each iteration, the position 𝜽=(x,y)\bm{\theta}=(x,y) evolves as

𝜽t+1=𝜽t−η⁡(∇ℒ​(𝜽t)+𝝃t),\bm{\theta}_{t+1}=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\eta\bigl(\nabla\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})+\bm{\xi}_{t}\bigr), (13)

where η\eta is the learning rate. The noise term 𝝃t\bm{\xi}_{t} is sampled from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution

𝝃t∼𝒩⁡(0,𝚺⁡(𝜽t)).\bm{\xi}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}(\bm{\theta}_{t})\bigr). (14)

In SGD, this gradient noise is empirically observed to be highly anisotropic and strongly correlated with the local geometry of the loss landscape [19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. To capture this landscape-dependent noise, we model the noise covariance as proportional to the local Hessian 𝐇⁡(𝜽t)\mathbf{H}(\bm{\theta}_{t}):

𝚺⁡(𝜽t)=2​σ​𝐇​(𝜽t),\mathbf{\Sigma}(\bm{\theta}_{t})=2\sigma\mathbf{H}(\bm{\theta}_{t}), (15)

where σ\sigma sets the noise strength, inversely dependent on batch size BB. Note that the qualitative behavior of our model is insensitive to the exact functional dependence between 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} and 𝐇\mathbf{H}. Any monotonically increasing relationship (e.g., 𝚺∝𝐇\mathbf{\Sigma}\propto\mathbf{H} or 𝚺∝𝐇2\mathbf{\Sigma}\propto\mathbf{H}^{2}) yields the same behavior (see Sec. II B in Supplemental Material and Fig. S6 for details).

Simulations of this model reproduce our key empirical findings. Starting from the two valleys with equal probabilities, we varied η\eta and σ\sigma and measured the probability of converging to the flatter valley PflatP_{\mathrm{flat}} and the normalized mean freezing time η​⟨tfreeze⟩\eta\langle t_{\mathrm{freeze}}\rangle, defined as the last valley-switching iteration (see Sec. II A in Supplemental Material for details). The results reveal a sharp transition: larger η\eta or σ\sigma dramatically increase the likelihood of convergence to the flatter valley (Fig. 5C), consistent with our empirical observation that stronger SGD noise biases solutions toward flatter minima (compare with Fig. 2F). Moreover, the model reproduces the link between noise and transient exploration. The normalized freezing time increases systematically with both η\eta and σ\sigma (Fig. 5D). This parallels our neural network experiments (compare with Fig. 3C).

Despite its simplicity, the two-valley model captures the essential features of the learning dynamics: the anisotropic landscape-dependent noise not only enables escape from sharper minima but also biases convergence toward flatter regions by extending the early transient exploration phase, thereby allowing the dynamics to settle preferentially into flatter solution valleys. Next, we analytically elucidate the underlying mechanisms for valley selection during the early exploratory learning phase in the two-valley model.

II.6 SGD favors flatter minima in the quasi–steady-state regime

In the limit of small learning rates, the discrete SGD updates in Eq. 13 can be approximated by a continuous-time stochastic process. In this regime, the learning dynamics are governed by a continuous-time Langevin equation, and the probability density P⁡(x,y,t)P(x,y,t) for the system to occupy position (x,y)(x,y) at time tt evolves according to a corresponding Fokker–Planck equation:

∂tP=∇⋅[P∇ℒ+𝐃⋅∇P].\partial_{t}P=\nabla\cdot\left[P\nabla\mathcal{L}+\mathbf{D}\cdot\nabla P\right]. (16)

The landscape-dependent noise leads to an anisotropic diffusion tensor 𝐃⁡(x,y)\mathbf{D}(x,y), expressed as

𝐃⁡(x,y)=12​η​𝚺​(x,y)=ΔS​𝐇​(x,y),\mathbf{D}(x,y)=\tfrac{1}{2}\eta\mathbf{\Sigma}(x,y)=\Delta_{S}\mathbf{H}(x,y), (17)

where the effective noise level of SGD is defined as the product of the learning rate and noise strength, i.e., ΔS≡η​σ\Delta_{S}\equiv\eta\sigma (see Appendix A.1 for details).

The dynamics involve several characteristic timescales: the local relaxation time in the xx-direction, τx∼f1​(2)​(y)\tau_{x}\sim f_{1(2)}(y), and the longitudinal drift time in the yy-direction, τy∼|d​y/d​t|−1\tau_{y}\sim|\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t|^{-1}. When τx≪τy\tau_{x}\ll\tau_{y}, the fast variable xx rapidly relaxes to a local equilibrium at an approximately fixed yy, which evolves at a much longer timescale. In this quasi-steady-state regime, the conditional probability distribution Pss±​(x|y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(x|y) takes the form:

Pss±​(x|y)≈1Zss±​(y)​exp⁡(ℒ0​(y)−ℒ​(x,y)D11±​(y)),P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(x|y)\approx\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(y)}\exp\!\left(\frac{\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)-\mathcal{L}(x,y)}{D_{11}^{\pm}(y)}\right), (18)

where D11±​(y)=2​ΔS/f1​(2)​(y)D_{11}^{\pm}(y)=2\Delta_{S}/f_{1(2)}(y) are the diffusion coefficients in the two valleys, and Zss±​(y)Z_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(y) are the corresponding normalization constants. Here and throughout, the superscripts “++” and “−-” denote quantities associated with the flatter and sharper valleys, respectively.

The landscape-dependent, anisotropic noise inherent to SGD violates the fluctuation–dissipation theorem, highlighting the intrinsically nonequilibrium nature of the learning dynamics. In the quasi–steady-state regime (τx≪τy)(\tau_{x}\ll\tau_{y}), the joint steady-state distribution can be approximated as Pss​(x,y)≈Pss​(x|y)​Pss​(y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}(x,y)\approx P_{\mathrm{ss}}(x|y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}(y). Solving for Pss​(x,y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}(x,y) reveals that the learning dynamics effectively explores a noise-induced nonequilibrium loss landscape, described by an effective potential ℒeff​(x,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}(x,y) that explicitly depends on the SGD noise strength:

ℒeff±​(x,y)≡−Teff​(y)​ln⁡Pss±​(x,y)≈γ±12​ℒ​(x,y)+(1−γ±12)​ℒ0​(y),\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\pm}(x,y)&\equiv-T_{\mathrm{eff}}(y)\ln P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(x,y)\\ &\approx\gamma^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{L}(x,y)+\left(1-\gamma^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}\right)\mathcal{L}_{0}(y),\end{split} (19)

where Teff​(y)≡D11+​(y)​D11−​(y)=2​ΔS/f1​(y)​f2​(y)T_{\mathrm{eff}}(y)\equiv\sqrt{D_{11}^{+}(y)D_{11}^{-}(y)}=2\Delta_{S}/\sqrt{f_{1}(y)f_{2}(y)} denotes the effective temperature.

This effective loss can be decomposed into the original loss ℒ⁡(x,y)\mathcal{L}(x,y) and an additional correction term ℒSGD​(x,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SGD}}(x,y) that arises solely from the anisotropic nature of the SGD noise (see Appendix A.2 for detailed derivation):

ℒSGD±​(x,y)≡ℒeff±​(x,y)−ℒ⁡(x,y)=(γ±12−1)​[ℒ⁡(x,y)−ℒ0​(y)].\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{\pm}(x,y)&\equiv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\pm}(x,y)-\mathcal{L}(x,y)\\ &=\left(\gamma^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}-1\right)\big[\mathcal{L}(x,y)-\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)\big].\end{split} (20)

Since the flatness ratio satisfies γ>1\gamma>1, the SGD correction term lowers the effective loss near the flat minimum while raising it near the sharp one, as shown in Fig. 6A.

To quantify the steady-state selection bias, we apply Kramers’ rate theory to estimate the escape rates from the sharp (kss−k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}) and flat (kss+k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}) valleys:

kss±​(y)≈[π2​f1​(2)​(y)​erfi​(Δ​ℒ​(y)​f1​(2)​(y)2​ΔS)]−1,k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(y)\approx\left[\frac{\pi}{2}f_{1(2)}(y)\,\mathrm{erfi}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}(y)f_{1(2)}(y)}{2\Delta_{S}}}\right)\right]^{-1}, (21)

where erfi⁡(⋅)\mathrm{erfi}(\cdot) denotes the imaginary error function, then the steady-state probability of converging to the flat valley at a particular value of yy is given by:

Pflatss,SGD​(y)≡kss−​(y)kss−​(y)+kss+​(y)=[1+γ−1​erfi⁡(Δ​ℒ​(y)​f2​(y)2​ΔS)erfi⁡(Δ​ℒ​(y)​f1​(y)2​ΔS)]−1≈[1+γ−12​exp⁡(Δ​ℒ​(y)​(f2​(y)−f1​(y))2​ΔS)]−1,\begin{split}P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{ss,SGD}}(y)&\equiv\frac{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}(y)}{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}(y)+k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}(y)}\\ &=\left[1+\gamma^{-1}\frac{\mathrm{erfi}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}(y)f_{2}(y)}{2\Delta_{S}}}\right)}{\mathrm{erfi}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}(y)f_{1}(y)}{2\Delta_{S}}}\right)}\right]^{-1}\\ &\approx\left[1+\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\left(\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}(y)(f_{2}(y)-f_{1}(y))}{2\Delta_{S}}\right)\right]^{-1},\end{split} (22)

where the approximation holds for ΔS≪Δ​ℒ​f1​(2)\Delta_{S}\ll\Delta\mathcal{L}f_{1(2)}. Since erfi⁡(⋅)\mathrm{erfi}(\cdot) is a monotonically increasing function, the nonequilibrium quasi-steady-state probability of being in the flat valley Pflatss,SGDP_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{ss,SGD}} always exceeds its equilibrium counterpart Pflateq=(1+γ−1)−1P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{eq}}=(1+\gamma^{-1})^{-1}:

Pflatss,SGD>Pflateq,P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{ss,SGD}}>P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{eq}}, (23)

confirming that anisotropic SGD noise enhances the likelihood of ending up in the flatter valley, consistent with previous theoretical work [21] (see Appendix A.3 for details).

II.7 Stronger SGD noise delays freezing and enhances search for flatter valleys

In the quasi-steady-state limit with a fixed yy, Eq. 22 predicts that increasing the global noise strength ΔS\Delta_{S} weakens the preference for the flatter valley, seemingly contradicting both our empirical results (Fig. 2F) and simulations (Fig. 5C). This apparent inconsistency arises because, at fixed yy, the effective loss (Eq. 19) is independent of ΔS\Delta_{S}; increasing the effective temperature therefore merely reduces valley selectivity. Resolving this paradox reveals a central insight of our study: final valley selection is not governed by a static equilibrium alone, but is critically shaped by the transient dynamics of yy. In particular, the value of yy at which Eq. 22 ultimately applies depends on the noise strength ΔS\Delta_{S}.

To see this, consider the transient valley-hopping dynamics, which is controlled by the inter-valley escape time τescape∼(kss++kss−)−1.\tau_{\mathrm{escape}}\sim(k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}+k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-})^{-1}. Early in learning, when the barrier between valleys is low, τescape≪τy\tau_{\mathrm{escape}}\ll\tau_{y}. In this regime, for small yy, the distribution rapidly equilibrates via frequent inter-valley hopping, yielding the steady-state probability given by Eq. 22. As yy increases, however, both the valley flatness f1​(2)​(y)f_{1(2)}(y) and the barrier height Δ​ℒ​(y)\Delta\mathcal{L}(y) grow, progressively suppressing escape. Eventually, the system reaches a “freezing point” yfreezey_{\mathrm{freeze}} at which inter-valley transitions effectively cease (Fig. 6B). The final valley occupation is therefore set by the quasi-steady-state distribution that becomes frozen at this point:

Pflattr,SGD≈[1+γ−12​exp⁡(x22−x122​ΔS​(yfreezeyb+yfreeze)2)]−1.P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{tr,SGD}}\approx\left[1+\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\!\left(\frac{x_{2}^{2}-x_{1}^{2}}{2\Delta_{S}}\left(\frac{y_{\mathrm{freeze}}}{y_{b}+y_{\mathrm{freeze}}}\right)^{2}\right)\right]^{-1}. (24)

One of our key findings is that the freezing point yfreezey_{\mathrm{freeze}} increases with the noise level ΔS\Delta_{S}. Intuitively, higher noise keeps the system “hotter” for longer, enabling continued inter-valley transitions and thus delaying the effective freezing point (Fig. 6B). Quantitatively, yfreezey_{\mathrm{freeze}} can be determined by requiring the escape rate from the sharper valley to become negligible compared to the evolution rate of the steady-state distribution, which leads to:

yfreeze≈yb⋅ΔS​ln⁡(ΔSε2​Φ2)x2−ΔS​ln⁡(ΔSε2​Φ2),y_{\mathrm{freeze}}\approx y_{b}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{S}\ln\left(\frac{\Delta_{S}}{\varepsilon^{2}\Phi^{2}}\right)}}{x_{2}-\sqrt{\Delta_{S}\ln\left(\frac{\Delta_{S}}{\varepsilon^{2}\Phi^{2}}\right)}}, (25)

where ε\varepsilon is a small quantity and Φ\Phi is a constant that absorbs other model parameters (see Appendix A.4 for detailed derivation). The dependence of yfreezey_{\mathrm{freeze}} on ΔS\Delta_{S} given in Eq. 25 explains the increased mean freezing time η​⟨tfreeze⟩\eta\langle t_{\mathrm{freeze}}\rangle with noise strength observed in both numerical simulations (Fig. 5D) and empirical deep network experiments (Fig. 3C). Plugging in the expression of yfreezey_{\mathrm{freeze}} for Pflattr,SGDP_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{tr,SGD}} (Eq. 24), we have:

Pflattr,SGD≈[1+γ−12​(ΔSε​Φ)1−γ]−1,P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{tr,SGD}}\approx\left[1+\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(\frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{S}}}{\varepsilon\Phi}\right)^{1-\gamma}\right]^{-1}, (26)

which clearly shows that the probability in the flat valley increases with noise strength.

Overall, while stronger noise decreases the steady-state preference for the flatter valley at a fixed yy by reducing the ratio kss+/kss−k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}/k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}, this static effect is dominated by a dynamic freezing mechanism. Increased noise delays the onset of freezing, allowing the system to explore the landscape for longer and ultimately leading to a greater probability of settling in the flatter valley at higher noise levels. This bias is further enhanced by a larger flatness contrast (γ=f1/f2>1\gamma=f_{1}/f_{2}>1), as shown in Fig. 6C. Together, these results provide a complete theoretical explanation for the observed positive correlation between noise strength and flat-valley selection, thereby resolving the apparent inconsistency arising from the steady-state analysis alone.

III Discussion

In this work, we investigated the early transient dynamics of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to uncover the physical mechanism underlying its preference for flatter, more generalizable solutions. Empirically, we find that the initial stage of training is highly exploratory, characterized by repeated transitions between distinct valleys of the loss landscape. During this phase, SGD frequently escapes sharper minima and migrates toward flatter regions, a process that is systematically enhanced by increased noise. These observations point to the early transient period as a decisive stage of optimization, during which solution selection is actively shaped.

We provide a physical explanation for this behavior based on a nonequilibrium mechanism. Anisotropic landscape-dependent noise in SGD reshapes the loss landscape by generating an effective potential that biases the dynamics toward flatter valleys. Crucially, however, the final outcome is not determined by a steady-state equilibrium alone. Instead, we identify a transient freezing process: as training proceeds, growing energy barriers and progressive valley flattening suppress inter-valley transitions, ultimately arresting exploration. Higher noise levels delay this freezing, thereby extending the temporal window over which the system can relax into flatter minima with superior generalization properties.

This mechanism is fundamentally distinct from previously proposed explanations based on dynamic instability, in which sharp minima become unstable and inaccessible at high learning rates [11]. By contrast, our results demonstrate that a robust bias toward flat minima emerges even when all valleys remain dynamically stable. In this regime, anisotropic stochasticity alone is sufficient to drive preferential selection through transient freezing. Our framework therefore explains how SGD favors flat solutions across a broad range of stable training conditions, without invoking instability or divergence.

Although our analytical treatment is based on a minimal two-dimensional model, its implications extend naturally to high-dimensional deep networks. In practice, optimization in deep learning is constrained to a highly degenerate, effectively low-dimensional submanifold of parameter space. Our model is designed to capture the essential degrees of freedom on this manifold: one corresponding to downhill loss minimization and another governing transitions between solutions of comparable loss separated by barriers. Within this reduced description, the same physical ingredients—noise-induced effective potentials followed by transient freezing—are expected to operate.

The framework further generalizes to realistic loss landscapes containing many competing valleys. Because the bias toward flatness strengthens with increasing curvature contrast (Fig. 6C), valley transitions are not purely stochastic but are directionally biased toward progressively flatter regions. Exploration continues along this directed path until it is halted by freezing. As a result, the optimizer is statistically guided to converge into one of the flattest valleys accessible during its noise-extended exploratory phase, providing a robust and physically grounded explanation for the emergence of generalizable solutions.

While our primary empirical analysis focuses on a multilayer perceptron trained on a simple dataset (MNIST), both the multi-valley structure of loss landscapes and the associated transient learning dynamics are widely observed across architectures and datasets [39, 40, 27, 30, 29]. To illustrate this generality, we present additional results for a convolutional neural network trained on CIFAR-10 in Supplemental Material, Sec. I F and Fig. S5.

Taken together, our results provide a unified physical framework connecting stochastic learning dynamics, loss-landscape geometry, and generalization. By identifying the early transient regime as the decisive stage of solution selection, we offer a dynamical explanation for the striking empirical success of SGD in deep learning. From this viewpoint, SGD does not merely locate a minimum; rather, it implements a noise-regulated selection process that systematically exploits landscape geometry to find flatter, more generalizable solutions.

Beyond conceptual insight, our results suggest concrete strategies for improving optimization and generalization by explicitly controlling early transient dynamics. In particular, learning-rate and batch-size schedules can be viewed as tools to regulate the duration of the exploratory phase before freezing, rather than just to ensure convergence. Actively shaping noise anisotropy or adaptively prolonging the transient regime may therefore enhance access to flatter, more robust solutions without compromising training instability. More broadly, our framework opens a path towards principled, dynamics-based design of stochastic optimization algorithms grounded in nonequilibrium statistical physics.

Appendix A Analytical results of the two-valley model

A.1 Continuous-time dynamics and Fokker-Planck equation

We analyze the continuous-time limit of the discrete SGD update rule:

𝜽t+1=𝜽t−η∇ℒ(𝜽t)−η𝝃t,\bm{\theta}_{t+1}=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\eta\nabla\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})-\eta\bm{\xi}_{t}, (A1)

where the gradient noise satisfies 𝔼⁡[𝝃t]=0\mathbb{E}[\bm{\xi}_{t}]=0 and Cov​[𝝃t]=𝚺⁡(𝜽t)\text{Cov}[\bm{\xi}_{t}]=\mathbf{\Sigma}(\bm{\theta}_{t}). By interpreting the learning rate η\eta as the discretization time step Δ​t\Delta t, the process converges to the following stochastic differential equation (SDE) in the limit η→0\eta\to 0 [22, 41]:

d𝜽t=𝐀⁡(𝜽t)​dt+2​𝐃​(𝜽t)​d𝐖t,\differential\bm{\theta}_{t}=\mathbf{A}(\bm{\theta}_{t})\differential t+\sqrt{2\mathbf{D}(\bm{\theta}_{t})}\differential\mathbf{W}_{t}, (A2)

where d𝐖t\differential\mathbf{W}_{t} denotes the standard Wiener increment. To determine the drift vector 𝐀\mathbf{A} and the diffusion tensor 𝐃\mathbf{D}, we match the first and second moments of the discrete update with those of the SDE:

  1. 1.

    Drift: Matching the deterministic components, 𝐀(𝜽)Δt=−η∇ℒ(𝜽)\mathbf{A}(\bm{\theta})\Delta t=-\eta\nabla\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}), yields:

    𝐀​(𝜽)=−∇ℒ​(𝜽).\mathbf{A}(\bm{\theta})=-\nabla\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}). (A3)
  2. 2.

    Diffusion: Matching the covariance of the noise terms, 2​𝐃​Δ​t=Cov​[−η​𝝃]2\mathbf{D}\Delta t=\text{Cov}[-\eta\bm{\xi}], implies 2​𝐃​η=η2​𝚺2\mathbf{D}\eta=\eta^{2}\mathbf{\Sigma}. This gives:

    𝐃⁡(𝜽)=12​η​𝚺​(𝜽).\mathbf{D}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{2}\eta\mathbf{\Sigma}(\bm{\theta}). (A4)

Under the assumption that the noise covariance is proportional to the Hessian, 𝚺⁡(𝜽)=2​σ​𝐇​(𝜽)\mathbf{\Sigma}(\bm{\theta})=2\sigma\mathbf{H}(\bm{\theta}), the diffusion tensor takes the form:

𝐃⁡(𝜽)=η​σ​𝐇​(𝜽)≡ΔS​𝐇​(𝜽),\mathbf{D}(\bm{\theta})=\eta\sigma\mathbf{H}(\bm{\theta})\equiv\Delta_{S}\mathbf{H}(\bm{\theta}), (A5)

where ΔS≡η​σ\Delta_{S}\equiv\eta\sigma represents the effective noise intensity.

The time evolution of the probability density P⁡(𝜽,t)P(\bm{\theta},t) is governed by the continuity equation ∂tP=−∇⋅𝐉\partial_{t}P=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J} [42]. Substituting the drift 𝐀=−∇ℒ\mathbf{A}=-\nabla\mathcal{L} and diffusion 𝐃\mathbf{D} into the probability current 𝐉=𝐀P−𝐃∇P\mathbf{J}=\mathbf{A}P-\mathbf{D}\nabla P, we obtain the Fokker-Planck equation:

∂tP(𝜽,t)=∇⋅[P(𝜽,t)∇ℒ(𝜽)+𝐃(𝜽)⋅∇P(𝜽,t)].\partial_{t}P(\bm{\theta},t)=\nabla\cdot\Big[P(\bm{\theta},t)\nabla\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})+\mathbf{D}(\bm{\theta})\cdot\nabla P(\bm{\theta},t)\Big]. (A6)

A.2 Non-equilibrium steady state and effective loss

Our derivation relies on the adiabatic approximation, the validity of which depends on a distinct separation of timescales between the fast transverse relaxation within the valleys (xx-direction) and the slow longitudinal drift (yy-direction).

The dynamics in the xx-direction are governed by the local curvature κx≡∂x2ℒ\kappa_{x}\equiv\partial_{x}^{2}\mathcal{L}. The characteristic transverse relaxation time τx\tau_{x}, representing the time required for the system to return to local equilibrium, is estimated as the inverse of this curvature:

τx​(y)≈(∂2ℒ∂x2)−1=12​f1​(2)​(y).\tau_{x}(y)\approx\left(\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{L}}{\partial x^{2}}\right)^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}f_{1(2)}(y). (A7)

Using the parameters f0=x0=1.0f_{0}=x_{0}=1.0 and x1=0.8x_{1}=0.8 from the simulation (Table. S1 of SM), the relaxation time is bounded by τxmax≈0.32\tau_{x}^{\mathrm{max}}\approx 0.32, which indicates a timescale of order 𝒪⁡(10−1)\mathcal{O}(10^{-1}). Conversely, the evolution of the slow variable yy is primarily driven by the global drift. The longitudinal drift timescale τy\tau_{y} is given by:

τy(y)=|dydt|−1≈[ℒdyde−y/yd+2​x02​yf​yf0​(y+yf)3]−1.\tau_{y}(y)=\left|\frac{\differential y}{\differential t}\right|^{-1}\approx\left[\frac{\mathcal{L}_{d}}{y_{d}}e^{-y/y_{d}}+\frac{2x_{0}^{2}y_{f}y}{f_{0}(y+y_{f})^{3}}\right]^{-1}. (A8)

With the simulation parameters, the minimum drift timescale is τymin≈41.8\tau_{y}^{\mathrm{min}}\approx 41.8. Comparing these conservative estimates yields a ratio of τx/τy∼7.6×10−3≪1\tau_{x}/\tau_{y}\sim 7.6\times 10^{-3}\ll 1. This vast separation justifies the adiabatic approximation.

Furthermore, given the block structure of the Hessian 𝐇\mathbf{H}, the diagonal elements dominate. Specifically, the cross-terms H12H_{12} are of order 𝒪⁡(1/yf,b)\mathcal{O}(1/y_{f,b}) and H22H_{22} is of order 𝒪⁡(1/yf,b2)\mathcal{O}(1/y_{f,b}^{2}), whereas H11H_{11} is of order 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1). Consequently, we approximate the diffusion matrix as diagonal, keeping only the dominant term in the xx-direction:

D11​(y)≈ΔS​H11​(x,y)={2​ΔS/f1​(y),x≥0,2​ΔS/f2​(y),x<0.D_{11}(y)\approx\Delta_{S}H_{11}(x,y)=\begin{cases}{2\Delta_{S}}/{f_{1}(y)},&x\geq 0,\\ {2\Delta_{S}}/{f_{2}(y)},&x<0.\end{cases} (A9)

Neglecting cross-diffusion terms, the Fokker-Planck equation for the conditional distribution in xx simplifies to:

∂tP⁡(x|y)≈∂x[P⁡(x|y)​∂xℒ⁡(x,y)+D11​(y)​∂xP⁡(x|y)].\partial_{t}P(x|y)\approx\partial_{x}\left[P(x|y)\partial_{x}\mathcal{L}(x,y)+D_{11}(y)\partial_{x}P(x|y)\right]. (A10)

Setting the probability flux to zero, the steady-state solution in each valley follows the Boltzmann form:

Pss±​(x|y)=1Zss±​(y)​exp⁡(−ℒ⁡(x,y)D11±​(y)),P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(x|y)=\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(y)}\exp\left(-\frac{\mathcal{L}(x,y)}{D_{11}^{\pm}(y)}\right), (A11)

where the superscripts ++ and −- denote the domains x≥0x\geq 0 (flatter valley) and x<0x<0 (sharper valley), respectively. Note that the effective temperature D11±D_{11}^{\pm} differs between the two valleys due to the Hessian-dependent noise.

Continuity of the probability density at the junction x=0x=0 requires Pss+​(0|y)=Pss−​(0|y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}(0|y)=P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}(0|y). Since ℒ​(0,y)=ℒ0​(y)\mathcal{L}(0,y)=\mathcal{L}_{0}(y), this condition implies the following relationship between the normalization constants:

Zss+​(y)Zss−​(y)=exp⁡[−ℒ0​(y)​(1D11+​(y)−1D11−​(y))].\frac{Z_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}(y)}{Z_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}(y)}=\exp\left[-\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)\left(\frac{1}{D_{11}^{+}(y)}-\frac{1}{D_{11}^{-}(y)}\right)\right]. (A12)

Assuming the drift in the yy-direction is sufficiently slow, the system reaches a non-equilibrium steady state in both directions. The marginal steady-state probability Pss​(y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}(y) is determined by the lowest-order approximation:

ddy[⟨∂yℒ⟩x+ddy​⟨D22⟩x+⟨D22⟩xddylnPss(y)]Pss(y)=0,\begin{split}\frac{\differential}{\differential y}\bigg[&\langle\partial_{y}\mathcal{L}\rangle_{x}+\frac{\differential}{\differential y}\langle D_{22}\rangle_{x}\\ &+\langle D_{22}\rangle_{x}\frac{\differential}{\differential y}\ln P_{\mathrm{ss}}(y)\bigg]P_{\mathrm{ss}}(y)=0,\end{split} (A13)

where ⟨⋅⟩x\langle\cdot\rangle_{x} denotes integration over the conditional steady-state distribution Pss±​(x|y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(x|y). The final joint steady-state probability Pss​(x,y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}(x,y) is then given by:

Pss±​(x,y)≡Pss±​(x|y)​Pss​(y)=1Zss​(y)​exp⁡(−ℒ​(x,y)−ℒ0​(y)D11±​(y)),\begin{split}P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(x,y)&\equiv P_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}(x|y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}(y)\\ &=\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm{ss}}(y)}\exp\left(-\frac{\mathcal{L}(x,y)-\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)}{D_{11}^{\pm}(y)}\right),\end{split} (A14)

where we have utilized the normalization relationship Eq. (A12) and absorbed all terms independent of xx into Zss​(y)Z_{\mathrm{ss}}(y).

To interpret this non-equilibrium steady state within the framework of equilibrium statistical mechanics, we define an effective loss ℒeff​(x,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}(x,y). We introduce a global effective temperature Teff​(y)T_{\mathrm{eff}}(y) for a fixed yy, defined as the geometric mean of the diffusion coefficients in the two valleys:

Teff​(y)≡D11+​(y)​D11−​(y)=2​ΔSf1​(y)​f2​(y).T_{\mathrm{eff}}(y)\equiv\sqrt{D_{11}^{+}(y)D_{11}^{-}(y)}=\frac{2\Delta_{S}}{\sqrt{f_{1}(y)f_{2}(y)}}. (A15)

The effective loss is defined via the Boltzmann relation Pss​(x,y)∝exp(−ℒeff(x,y)/Teff)P_{\mathrm{ss}}(x,y)\propto\exp(-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}(x,y) / T_{\mathrm{eff}}). Substituting the derived expression for Pss​(x,y)P_{\mathrm{ss}}(x,y), we obtain:

ℒeff±​(x,y)≡−Teff​ln⁡Pss±​(x,y)=TeffD11±​[ℒ⁡(x,y)−ℒ0​(y)]+ℒ0​(y)+Teff​ln⁡Zss​(y).\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\pm}(x,y)&\equiv-T_{\mathrm{eff}}\ln P^{\pm}_{\mathrm{ss}}(x,y)\\ &=\frac{T_{\mathrm{eff}}}{D_{11}^{\pm}}\left[\mathcal{L}(x,y)-\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)\right]\\ &\quad+\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)+T_{\mathrm{eff}}\ln Z_{\mathrm{ss}}(y).\end{split} (A16)

By imposing the condition ℒeff​(0,y)=ℒ0​(y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}(0,y)=\mathcal{L}_{0}(y), regardless the uniform term Teff​ln⁡Zss​(y)T_{\mathrm{eff}}\ln Z_{\mathrm{ss}}(y) for fixed yy, we recover Eq. 19 of the main text:

ℒeff±​(x,y)≈f1​(2)f2​(1)​ℒ​(x,y)+(1−f1​(2)f2​(1))​ℒ0​(y)=γ±12​ℒ​(x,y)+(1−γ±12)​ℒ0​(y).\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\pm}(x,y)&\approx\sqrt{\frac{f_{1(2)}}{f_{2(1)}}}\,\mathcal{L}(x,y)+\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{f_{1(2)}}{f_{2(1)}}}\right)\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)\\ &=\gamma^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{L}(x,y)+\left(1-\gamma^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}\right)\mathcal{L}_{0}(y).\end{split} (A17)

We can thus decompose the effective loss into the original loss plus an SGD-induced correction term:

ℒSGD±​(x,y)≡ℒeff±​(x,y)−ℒ⁡(x,y)=(γ±12−1)​[ℒ⁡(x,y)−ℒ0​(y)].\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{\pm}(x,y)&\equiv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\pm}(x,y)-\mathcal{L}(x,y)\\ &=\left(\gamma^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}-1\right)\big[\mathcal{L}(x,y)-\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)\big].\end{split} (A18)

Note that inside the valleys, the term [ℒ⁡(x,y)−ℒ0​(y)][\mathcal{L}(x,y)-\mathcal{L}_{0}(y)] is strictly negative. For the flatter valley (x>0x>0), the condition γ≡f1/f2>1\gamma\equiv f_{1}/f_{2}>1 implies a positive prefactor (γ1/2−1)>0(\gamma^{1/2}-1)>0. Consequently, the SGD correction ℒSGD+<0\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{+}<0, which effectively deepens the potential well. Conversely, for the sharper valley (x<0x<0), the prefactor becomes negative since (γ−1/2−1)<0(\gamma^{-1/2}-1)<0. This results in a positive correction ℒSGD−>0\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{-}>0, which effectively raises the potential well.

A.3 Kramers’ escape rates and steady-state convergence probability

We quantify inter-valley transitions using the Mean First Passage Time (MFPT) [42]. Based on the Fokker-Planck equation, the MFPT from the sharp valley minimum (x2⋆x_{2}^{\star}) to the barrier (x=0x=0), denoted τs→f\tau_{s\to f}, is:

τs→f=1D11−​∫x2⋆0dx′​eℒ⁡(x′)D11−​∫−∞x′dx′′​e−ℒ⁡(x′′)D11−.\tau_{s\to f}=\frac{1}{D_{11}^{-}}\int_{x_{2}^{\star}}^{0}\differential x^{\prime}e^{\frac{\mathcal{L}(x^{\prime})}{D_{11}^{-}}}\int_{-\infty}^{x^{\prime}}\differential x^{\prime\prime}e^{-\frac{\mathcal{L}(x^{\prime\prime})}{D_{11}^{-}}}. (A19)

Similarly, for the transition from the flat valley minimum (x1⋆x_{1}^{\star}) to the sharp side (τf→s\tau_{f\to s}):

τf→s=1D11+​∫0x1⋆dx′​eℒ⁡(x′)D11+​∫x′+∞dx′′​e−ℒ⁡(x′′)D11+.\tau_{f\to s}=\frac{1}{D_{11}^{+}}\int_{0}^{x_{1}^{\star}}\differential x^{\prime}e^{\frac{\mathcal{L}(x^{\prime})}{D_{11}^{+}}}\int_{x^{\prime}}^{+\infty}\differential x^{\prime\prime}e^{-\frac{\mathcal{L}(x^{\prime\prime})}{D_{11}^{+}}}. (A20)

We apply Kramers’ approximation, assuming rare escape events. This regime holds when the noise amplitude is small relative to the barrier height (D11±≪Δ​ℒD_{11}^{\pm}\ll\Delta\mathcal{L}), satisfying:

ΔS≪12​(x1​(2)​yy+yb)2.\Delta_{S}\ll\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x_{1(2)}y}{y+y_{b}}\right)^{2}. (A21)

In this limit, the double integrals decouple. The inner integral is evaluated via the Gaussian approximation around the potential minimum (x′′≈x2⋆x^{\prime\prime}\approx x_{2}^{\star}):

∫−∞+∞dx′′exp⁡(−1D11−​[x′′​(x′′+g2)f2+ℒ0])≈π​D11−​f2e−ℒ(x2⋆,y)/D11−.\begin{split}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\differential x^{\prime\prime}&\exp\left({-\frac{1}{D_{11}^{-}}\left[\frac{x^{\prime\prime}(x^{\prime\prime}+g_{2})}{f_{2}}+\mathcal{L}_{0}\right]}\right)\\ &\approx\sqrt{\pi D_{11}^{-}f_{2}}e^{-\mathcal{L}(x_{2}^{\star},y)/D_{11}^{-}}.\end{split} (A22)

The outer integral is dominated by the region near the barrier top (x′→0x^{\prime}\to 0), yielding:

∫x2⋆0dx′exp⁡(1D11−​[x′​(x′+g2)f2+ℒ0])=π​D11−​f22​eℒ⁡(x2⋆,y)/D11−​erfi​(Δ​ℒD11−),\begin{split}\int_{x_{2}^{\star}}^{0}\differential x^{\prime}&\exp\left({\frac{1}{D_{11}^{-}}\left[\frac{x^{\prime}(x^{\prime}+g_{2})}{f_{2}}+\mathcal{L}_{0}\right]}\right)\\ &=\frac{\sqrt{\pi D_{11}^{-}f_{2}}}{2}e^{\mathcal{L}(x_{2}^{\star},y)/D_{11}^{-}}\,\mathrm{erfi}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}}{D_{11}^{-}}}\right),\end{split} (A23)

where erfi⁡(z)\mathrm{erfi}(z) is the imaginary error function. Applying the same derivation to τf→s\tau_{f\to s}, the analytical MFPTs are:

τf→s\displaystyle\tau_{f\to s} ≈π2​f1​(y)​erfi​[Δ​ℒ​(y)​f1​(y)2​ΔS],\displaystyle\approx\frac{\pi}{2}f_{1}(y)\,\mathrm{erfi}\left[\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}(y)f_{1}(y)}{2\Delta_{S}}}\right], (A24)
τs→f\displaystyle\tau_{s\to f} ≈π2​f2​(y)​erfi​[Δ​ℒ​(y)​f2​(y)2​ΔS].\displaystyle\approx\frac{\pi}{2}f_{2}(y)\,\mathrm{erfi}\left[\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}(y)f_{2}(y)}{2\Delta_{S}}}\right].

Using the asymptotic expansion erfi⁡(z)≈ez2/(π​z)\mathrm{erfi}(z)\approx e^{z^{2}}/(\sqrt{\pi}z) for z≫1z\gg 1, the escape rates kss±≡1/τf⁡(s)→s⁡(f)k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{\pm}\equiv 1/\tau_{f(s)\to s(f)} become:

kss+\displaystyle k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+} ≈2​Δ​ℒπ​ΔS​f1​exp⁡[−Δ​ℒ​f12​ΔS],\displaystyle\approx\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta\mathcal{L}}{\pi\Delta_{S}f_{1}}}\exp\left[-\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}f_{1}}{2\Delta_{S}}\right], (A25)
kss−\displaystyle k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-} ≈2​Δ​ℒπ​ΔS​f2​exp⁡[−Δ​ℒ​f22​ΔS].\displaystyle\approx\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta\mathcal{L}}{\pi\Delta_{S}f_{2}}}\exp\left[-\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}f_{2}}{2\Delta_{S}}\right].

The probability evolution follows the master equation:

dPflatdt\displaystyle\frac{\differential P_{\mathrm{flat}}}{\differential t} =kss−​Psharp−kss+​Pflat,\displaystyle=k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}P_{\mathrm{sharp}}-k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}P_{\mathrm{flat}}, (A26)
dPsharpdt\displaystyle\frac{\differential P_{\mathrm{sharp}}}{\differential t} =kss+​Pflat−kss−​Psharp.\displaystyle=k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}P_{\mathrm{flat}}-k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}P_{\mathrm{sharp}}.

The steady-state probability of residing in the flat valley, Pflatss,SGD=kss−/(kss−+kss+)P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{ss,SGD}}=k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}/(k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}+k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}), is given by:

Pflatss,SGD=[1+γ−1​erfi⁡(Δ​ℒ​f22​ΔS)erfi⁡(Δ​ℒ​f12​ΔS)]−1≈[1+γ−12​exp⁡(Δ​ℒ​(f2−f1)2​ΔS)]−1.\begin{split}P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{ss,SGD}}&=\left[1+\gamma^{-1}\frac{\mathrm{erfi}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}f_{2}}{2\Delta_{S}}}\right)}{\mathrm{erfi}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}f_{1}}{2\Delta_{S}}}\right)}\right]^{-1}\\ &\approx\left[1+\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\left(\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}(f_{2}-f_{1})}{2\Delta_{S}}\right)\right]^{-1}.\end{split} (A27)

For isotropic noise (D11+=D11−D_{11}^{+}=D_{11}^{-}), the effective temperature is uniform, and Eq. (22) reduces to the equilibrium distribution:

Pflateq=(1+f2​(y)f1​(y))−1=γ1+γ.P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{eq}}=\left(1+\frac{f_{2}(y)}{f_{1}(y)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma}. (A28)

Comparing Eq. (A27) and Eq. (A28) confirms that SGD noise introduces a significant bias (Pflatss,SGD>PflateqP_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{ss,SGD}}>P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{eq}}) due to the super-linear growth of erfi⁡(z)\mathrm{erfi}(z), amplifying geometric differences between valleys.

A.4 The freezing mechanism and transient dynamics approximation

The final solution selection is governed by the competition between inter-valley diffusion and longitudinal drift. As yy increases, the escape rates k±k^{\pm} decrease exponentially. The system ”freezes” when the transition timescale exceeds the drift timescale. The final probability is approximated by the quasi-steady distribution at the freezing point yfreezey_{\mathrm{freeze}}:

Pflattr,SGD≈[1+γ−12​exp⁡(Δ​ℒ​[f2−f1]2​ΔS)]−1|yfreeze=[1+γ−12​exp⁡(x22−x122​ΔS​(yfreezeyb+yfreeze)2)]−1,\begin{split}P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{tr,SGD}}&\approx\left[1+\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\left(\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}[f_{2}-f_{1}]}{2\Delta_{S}}\right)\right]^{-1}\bigg|_{y_{\mathrm{freeze}}}\\ &=\left[1+\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\!\left(\frac{x_{2}^{2}-x_{1}^{2}}{2\Delta_{S}}\left(\frac{y_{\mathrm{freeze}}}{y_{b}+y_{\mathrm{freeze}}}\right)^{2}\right)\right]^{-1},\end{split} (A29)

where we have substituted the definitions of Δ​ℒ\Delta\mathcal{L}, f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}.

We define the freezing point yfreezey_{\mathrm{freeze}} as the juncture where the escape rate from the sharper valley becomes significantly smaller than the rate of change of the steady-state distribution (kss−≈ε​|P˙/P|k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}\approx\varepsilon|\dot{P}/P|):

kss−≈−ε​(1+kss+kss−)−1​dd​t​(kss+kss−),k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}\approx-\varepsilon\left(1+\frac{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}}{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}}\right)^{-1}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}}{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}}\right), (A30)

where ε\varepsilon is a small constant. We expand the time derivative term using the chain rule:

dd​t​(kss+kss−)≈kss+2​ΔS​kss−​dd​y​[Δ​ℒ​(f2−f1)]​y˙≈−kss+2​ΔS​kss−[ℒdyde−y/yd+…]×[(x12−x22)​yb​y(y+yb)3].\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}}{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}}\right)&\approx\frac{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}}{2\Delta_{S}k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}\Bigl[\Delta\mathcal{L}\bigl(f_{2}-f_{1}\bigr)\Bigr]\dot{y}\\ &\approx-\frac{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}}{2\Delta_{S}k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}}\left[\frac{\mathcal{L}_{d}}{y_{d}}e^{-y/y_{d}}+\dots\right]\\ &\quad\times\left[\frac{(x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2})y_{b}y}{(y+y_{b})^{3}}\right].\end{split} (A31)

Inserting this derivative back into the freezing criterion Eq. (A30) yields:

kss−≈ε​ΦΔS​kss+kss++kss−.k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}\approx\frac{\varepsilon\Phi}{\Delta_{S}}\frac{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}}{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}+k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}}. (A32)

Here, all model parameters are absorbed into Φ\Phi. We focus on the regime where freezing occurs well before Pflattr,SGDP_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{tr,SGD}} reaches 1, so that kss−/kss+=𝒪⁡(1)k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}/k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{+}=\mathcal{O}(1). In this regime, the escape rates decay exponentially with yy, much faster than the polynomial decay of Φ\Phi. We therefore approximate Φ\Phi by its upper bound and treat it as an effective constant:

Φ≡12[ℒdyde−y/yd+…][(x12−x22)​yb​y(y+yb)3]≈2​(x12−x22)27​yb​(ℒdyd+8​x0227​yf).\begin{split}\Phi&\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\mathcal{L}_{d}}{y_{d}}e^{-y/y_{d}}+\dots\right]\left[\frac{(x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2})y_{b}y}{(y+y_{b})^{3}}\right]\\ &\approx\frac{2(x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2})}{27y_{b}}\left(\frac{\mathcal{L}_{d}}{y_{d}}+\frac{8x_{0}^{2}}{27y_{f}}\right).\end{split} (A33)

This simplifies the relation to kss−≈ε​Φ/ΔS{k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-}}\approx\varepsilon\Phi/\Delta_{S}. Substituting the explicit exponential form of kss−k_{\mathrm{ss}}^{-} (Eq. A25), the freezing criterion becomes:

2​Δ​ℒπ​ΔS​f2​exp⁡[−Δ​ℒ​f22​ΔS]≈ε​ΦΔS.\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta\mathcal{L}}{\pi\Delta_{S}f_{2}}}\exp\left[-\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}f_{2}}{2\Delta_{S}}\right]\approx\frac{\varepsilon\Phi}{\Delta_{S}}. (A34)

Assuming the prefactor varies slowly, we solve the implicit equation for the exponent:

Δ​ℒ​(yfreeze)​f2​(yfreeze)2​ΔS≈x222​ΔS​(yfreezeyb+yfreeze)2≈ln⁡(ΔSε​Φ).\begin{split}\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}(y_{\mathrm{freeze}})f_{2}(y_{\mathrm{freeze}})}{2\Delta_{S}}&\approx\frac{x_{2}^{2}}{2\Delta_{S}}\left(\frac{y_{\mathrm{freeze}}}{y_{b}+y_{\mathrm{freeze}}}\right)^{2}\\ &\approx\ln\left(\frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{S}}}{\varepsilon\Phi}\right).\end{split} (A35)

Solving for yfreezey_{\mathrm{freeze}} reveals its explicit dependence on noise strength:

yfreeze≈yb⋅ΔS​ln⁡(ΔSε2​Φ2)x2−ΔS​ln⁡(ΔSε2​Φ2).y_{\mathrm{freeze}}\approx y_{b}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{S}\ln\left(\frac{\Delta_{S}}{\varepsilon^{2}\Phi^{2}}\right)}}{x_{2}-\sqrt{\Delta_{S}\ln\left(\frac{\Delta_{S}}{\varepsilon^{2}\Phi^{2}}\right)}}. (A36)

Substituting Eq. (A36) back into Eq. (A29), we obtain the final transient probability:

Pflattr,SGD≈[1+γ−12​exp⁡(x22−x12x22​ln⁡(ΔSε​Φ))]−1≈[1+γ−12​(ΔSε​Φ)1−γ]−1.\begin{split}P_{\mathrm{flat}}^{\mathrm{tr,SGD}}&\approx\left[1+\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\!\left(\frac{x_{2}^{2}-x_{1}^{2}}{x_{2}^{2}}\ln\left(\frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{S}}}{\varepsilon\Phi}\right)\right)\right]^{-1}\\ &\approx\left[1+\gamma^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(\frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{S}}}{\varepsilon\Phi}\right)^{1-\gamma}\right]^{-1}.\end{split} (A37)

Since γ=f1/f2>1\gamma=f_{1}/f_{2}>1, the exponent (1−γ)(1-\gamma) is negative. Thus, increasing noise ΔS\Delta_{S} reduces the term in the denominator, thereby increasing the probability PflatP_{\mathrm{flat}} of selecting the flatter valley.
